properties.text: Painted mural on both sides of Metra underpass on Elston. It features images of flore and fauna of the area thru the four season. This mural was funded by local businesses and painted with the help of community residents.

Since we have gardens on three sides of our home, we chose a garden theme for the fourth side ;-)

properties.name: 63rd Street Gateway
properties.text: Green Star Movement, with the help of approximately 500 volunteers, created this mosaic to celebrate the Woodlawn neighborhood and its culture. Elaborate portraits of notable figures, including Barack Obama, Michelle Obama, and singer Minnie Riperton are shaped out of tile. Photographs embedded in the material memorialize other former residents—including Emmett Till and Muhammad Ali. Further highlighting Woodlawn’s rich history, imagery from the front page of the Chicago Crusader, a newspaper headquartered in the neighborhood, is prominently displayed within the mosaic.

properties.name: 63rd and Infinity
properties.text: In creating the mural with spray paint for Boombox Englewood, Matt Sansing has depicted a silhouette of a different Chicago skyline, featuring elements within the surrounding blocks in Englewood. This location is one of four Boombox installations across the city managed by Latent Design. This project was realized in partnership with the People Plazas program of the Chicago Department of Transportation’s Make Way for People initiative, and the Department of Planning and Development’s Retail Thrive Zone program.

properties.name: Abrazando La Vida/Embracing Life
properties.text: This mural’s positive symbolism, coupled with the strong use of primary colors, intends to bring a reflective energy to the location as a reminder to balance our mind, matter, and soul.

properties.name: Abstract Botanical City
properties.text: As my partner Bob Buchholz was spray painting over some gang tags on the outer front wall of our apartment building, our landlord Tom Nizinski was walking by with his dog. Tom asked Bob, "Would Diane like to do a mural?" When Bob relayed the invitation to paint the building I was electrified with enthusiasm! Seemed like a win/win opportunity to me and the building owners! Our landlords covered the cost of paint. I gave them a few watercolor painting designs from which to choose preferences, and Bob helped me with chalk lining, grid drawing, priming, measuring and helping out with the ladder. I painted in all the details. It was a great relief to have such a monumental creative endeavor happening on such a great scale in our own neighborhood, on our own dwelling place during the pandemic! And where there is art...there are no gang tags. That's the long known "law" among the gangs. "More Art Less Tags" we say! There is also a shrine in the doorway by my partner, Robert Buchholz. His artwork is primarily found object assemblages.

properties.name: Asherah Bouquet
properties.text: Asherah is the mother goddess of the Canaanite pantheon, but this mural depicts Chicago-native Sarah Ratissi draped in flowers plucked from a realm between the city's natural ecosystem and the collective's half-forgotten dreams. When Caesar and his friends were coming up in Chicago's creative scene, Estelle's was a favorite haunt of the old nightlife stomping grounds in Wicker Park. Ashera Bouquet marks the latest installment of an ongoing series in Caesar's mural practice where he depicts women he admires as idols inspired by cross-cultural goddesses. This offering to both the local community and precious memories now blooms a full four stories tall, welcoming revelers on train and foot with a friendly gaze and the Car Prz signature, eye-catching electric color palette. This mural was sponsored and funded by Wicker Park Bucktown Special Service Area #33.

properties.name: Audubon Mural Project
properties.word: Mural · 2016 · Ruben Aguirre, Cheri Charlton. Andrea Jablonski, Anthony Lewellen, Tyrue Slang Jones, Chris Silva
properties.text: In 2016 the Mile of Murals collaborated with New York's Audubon Mural Project to pilot the Chicago edition. The Audubon Mural Project began in 2014 as a public art initiative of the National Audubon Society, in partnership with the Harlem-based Gitler &_____ Gallery of upper Manhattan, New York. The goal of the project is to paint murals honoring North American bird species that Audubon’s research has determined are threatened by climate change in this century, in order to bring awareness to this environmental crisis. A report published in 2014 found that 314 North American bird species will be severely threatened by future climate change. By 2080, these species are projected to lose at least half of their current climatic ranges as conditions (especially temperature and precipitation) become unsuitable for their continued survival. For this project, the Mile of Murals team worked closely with the Audubon Great Lakes Regional Office to identify birds within the Chicago area region that are threatened, across six habitat categories. The birds featured in these murals include the Tree Swallow, Baltimore Oriole, Peregrine Falcon, Bald Eagle, Hooded Merganser, Mallard, and Wood Duck, Black Crowned Night Heron, Black Cormorant, Yellow Bellied Sapsucker, Hairy Woodpecker, Red-breasted Nuthatch, and White-breasted Nuthatch.

properties.name: Baseball Rules
properties.text: The south wall, “Baseball Rules” is based on a movie quote, “There is only three rules in baseball: you throw the ball, you hit the ball, you catch the ball” with images of Jack McDonald pitching, Frank Thomas hitting and Carleton Fisk, and Dwayne Wise.

properties.name: Be Happy
properties.text: Be Happy is a collaboration between collage artist Thomas Kong and the Roman Susan Art Foundation in Rogers Park. Kong is the proprietor of Kim's Foods, on the corner of Estes and Glenwood at the heart of the Mile of Murals. A group of artists helped to create a public mural situated immediately outside Kim’s Corner Food to honor his contributions to the cultural vitality of the neighborhood.

properties.name: Be The Change You Want To See
properties.text: French artist, Kashink, is known for painting large four-eyes characters, using bright colors and thick lines. She says she likes exploring the absurdity of social interactions through the theme of masks, the taboo of death and the various ways of dealing with it, especially in the Latino culture. Kashink is also known for wearing a mustache, much like the images she creates. Thanks to Chicago Truborn Gallery for curating this piece. “Be The Change” (above Kashnik’s piece) painted by Stuk One.

properties.name: Becoming
properties.word: Mural · 2017 · Northwest Arts Connection with AnySquared Projects Tracy Kostenbader, Rosa Pineda, and Holiday Gerry
properties.text: Part of the 30th Ward is a former industrial corridor that is becoming residential. The Artists who created these murals responded to the question, “What does urban renewal or urban evolution mean to this area?”

properties.name: Bend

properties.name: Big Fruit
properties.text: From the very beginning, the mural’s intention was to radiate themes of ‘life’, ‘growth’ and ‘bright future’. The over-saturated aquamarine leaves and large red fruit are meant to evoke feelings of fertile soil. The very name of the mural, “Big Fruit”, is a play on the names given to other towns or cities. As if to say, “Howard Street, Land of the Big Fruit”, where people can settle, grow and happily sustain. Fischer also thought that the bold, lively color scheme would cut through the drearier winter days as commuters waited on the 2nd busiest train platform in the city.

properties.name: Bike-Family
properties.text: This mural was painted on the back wall of a new bike corral at the Lunt Ave. entrance of the Morse EL station on the CTA Red line. The theme for the wall was a general call for Bicycle Transportation, and artist Bruno Carneiro Mosciaro, aka Bruno Big, an artist based in Rio De Janeiro, won the commission. In "Bike-­?Family", Bruno Big approached the theme of using Bicycles as a collective joyful experience and integrating people with the environment and among themselves. The idea of depicting a family riding a bicycle is also a way of transforming the model of families owning a car and this being the main source of transportation and demonstrating that the act of riding a bicycle can be fun. Bruno Big works in a variety of media and is known for his vibrant colors and large forms that capture the subtle poetry of motion, the vivid pulse of life, and the dark mystery of death.

From 1993

properties.text: The mural is an allegory of freedom and the teaching of love. It represents traveling souls, migration, and the home we all carry. The birds I depicted on the wall are endemic to Mexico's northern Pacific coast; they are called the beautiful black-throated magpie. I am inspired by nature, especially birds, because of what they symbolize: diversity, identity, and freedom.

properties.name: Chicago is a whole new world
properties.text: The mural titled *"Chicago is a Whole New World"* vividly captures the spirit of Mahalia Jackson, the legendary gospel singer, as she rises above the city of Chicago, symbolizing both her roots and the transformative power of music. Set against a backdrop of Chicago’s iconic skyline, Jackson is depicted with her arms outstretched, her powerful voice seemingly reaching the heavens. The mural combines vibrant colors and dynamic brushstrokes, blending the soul of gospel with the city’s rich cultural heritage. It celebrates Jackson's role in shaping the city's musical landscape and her impact on the world.

properties.name: Chicago- Wind, Sun, and Shine
properties.text: A native of Chicago, Zimmermann has achieved national and international recognition for his large-scale murals featuring painted images of contemporary pop culture and sensitively rendered portraits. His pop-culture references range from innocuous consumer products such as beer cans, hard candy rings, and high-heeled shoes, to more symbolically charged images like pistols and portraits of political figures. The images are discrete and floating, knitted together by geometric areas of flat color. The overall aesthetic is smooth and sensual: shiny metal and glossy surfaces, rendered in saturated colors.

Come to Light
properties.text: Completed: 2011 Artist: Andy Bellomo, Brett Whitacre Come to Light, was designed to represent a change in light over the course of a day and also the change that happens within each of us. From one wall to the next wall, The artist wanted the size, color, shape, and details of the piece to change as it traveled from one wall through the second and to the last one.

properties.name: Community Assets: Love and Hope
properties.text: The mural is part of a larger community art initiative at ACCESS, focused on beautifying the neighborhoods where ACCESS health centers are located to reflect the culture of their surrounding communities. ACCESS believes in the humanizing andâ€¯healing powers of art and wants to support local artists in bringing art to our underinvested communities and make art more accessible to all. The ACCESS Westside mural is the first art installment of a larger initiative, with the goal of bringing public art to every region that ACCESS serves. With the support from the ACCESS Community Art Project Committee of staff and patients, local artist Miguel A. Del Realâ€¯was selected due to his personal connection to the Lawndale community and strong work around cultural inclusion. With Del Realâ€™s collaborative process, ACCESS brought in ACCESS Westsideâ€™s manager and the centerâ€™s care team and patients, as well as community partners, local businesses, to provide vital feedback on themes, colors, and words that represent the community. Through this collaborative process, key topics were highlighted in the muralâ€™s theme and design.

properties.name: Community Is...
properties.text: As part of the 2024 Together We Heal project (DCASE), Mandala Arts, artist Indira Freitas Johnson, engaged residents of Rogers Park in exploring the meaning of 'community' through the process of mural making. Through a month-long process in May 2024, participants identified words, symbols and colors to represent the spirit of Devon Avenue and Rogers Park and paint it onto the exterior wall of the Republic Bank of Chicago. Participants met at the Hamdard Health Alliance for weekly meetings and become part of Mandala's Devon Community Advisory Council, which was set up to reflect the needs and desires of the people of Devon through art and culture. The project marked the finale of the sixth edition of the Mandala Makers Festival, an annual program to bring art into the public spaces of Devon.

properties.name: Community Mosiac
properties.text: This mosaic is comprised of tile and grouting, showing leaves, snowflakes, foliage, and other seasonal elements against a yellow background. In the background, the CTA 'L' tracks and train are depicted, along with signage for Southport and Paulina stations.

properties.name: Continuing the Journey
properties.text: Echoing Iriving Park Lutheran Church's logo and the painting behind the altar, "Continuing the Journey" evokes the church's core values of welcoming all as they are in Christ's name on a shared journey of faith.

properties.name: CoyWolf
properties.text: In CoyWolf, two large animals patterned with vibrant shapes stare at the viewer with boldly colored eyes. The coyote/wolf hybrids depicted in the mural now stand as icons of The 606, the nearby innovative public recreation space.

properties.name: Creative Collective
properties.text: The mural reflects the inspiration of young artists, business owners and entrepreneurs in the area while tipping a hat to the rich history of Chicago at the same time. Matt Bourque says, “I’m borrowing from the existing architecture of the building. The history is already here so my job is to bring new life to this foundation. I cannot represent every ethnicity, culture or way of thinking, but I can treat each window with a different sensibility to reflect my respect.” Bourque continues ” I am really painting the dynamics of a working, growing community. I am inspired by the efforts of the hard-working people and culture around me.”

The piece is a reimagining of Jitish Kallat’s Public Notice 3, based on comments regarding the evolution and devolution of religious tolerance over the last two centuries.

(Photo Credit: Sandra Steinbrecher) Ruben Aguirre is a Chicago-based painter who has transitioned from graffiti writing to an abstract/contemporary muralist.
While working on this project Aguirre stated, “The first inspiration is the space itself. My work is a response to a site specific place, so looking, thinking and reacting with paint is the result of being there.” – as quoted in Sandra Steinbrecher’s Wabash Arts Corridor / Big Walls / 2016

properties.name: Educators & Workers & Steel in South Chicago
properties.text: Recognized now as an important Chicago artist, Vincent Mendoza graduated from Bowen in 1968. In 1975 he painted a large wall mural that gives us pride in our school and community. The center of the mural shows a steel mill blast furnace fiery colors. South Chicago workers and educators make a human story for the mural. The Calumet River brings heavy cargo ships into the steel mill ports.

properties.name: El Abrazo
properties.word: Mural · 2017 · El Paseo Community Garden with Eric J. Garcia, Diana Solís, Katia Péres-Fuentes
properties.text: During the development of the mural El Abrazo—which translates to “The Embrace” in Spanish—25th Ward residents offered concepts of immigration, migration, borders, agriculture and environment. Project Artists worked with five teenage apprentices—Natalie Alicea, Natalie Aparicio, Yazmin Jiminez, Jasmin Martinez, and Jocelyn Tlapa—to form the multigenerational team that painted the mural.

properties.name: Energy Conversion
properties.text: General idea is to honor the electrical workers by depicting the bending, positioning and angles that are required to manipulate the pipes for electricity. There's also the duality of male and female figures represented as professionals in their Craft/trade. The abstract piece in the middle is based on Tesla's AC/DC motor which he invented that allowed current to flow both ways; the patterns symbolize energy. The mural overall illustrates the human manipulation of energy and how we concentrate it for our own benefit and lighting the world.

properties.name: FLOW
properties.text: An abstract color theory mural with pixellated gradients of color mapped to a Roman block wall. The work is a contemporary example of abstract Impressionism and is inspired by the early video game and graphics development of Chicago's history (Midway Games et al). The work features smooth, pixellated color gradients which depict the flow of water and the reversal of the flow of the Chicago River, as well as a large, abstract "Irish Eye" to commemorate the Irish immigrants who died reversing the flow of the Chicago River in this historically Irish Bridgeport riverfront location. The mural also features ancient geometries found in Chicago's historic brick facades and in Mitla, Oaxaca, Mexico---the artist's nod to the Mexican heritage of the Pilsen neighborhood it faces.

properties.name: Fabric of Our Lives
properties.word: Mural · 1980 · Miriam Socoloff and Cynthia Weiss
properties.text: Artists Miriam Socoloff and Cynthia Weiss. 1980. Located at the Bernard Horwich Jewish Community Center, this ceramic and glass tile mosaic represents Jewish history in Chicago, a theme long neglected in Chicago's many historical murals. From 1980 )

properties.name: Face Lift
properties.text: The face is designed to inspire viewers from the ground and from the hotel across the alley. From both, you have a clear point of view of the mural, it's colors and one of the most inspiring things we can see almost daily, the sky. This mural was created for ACTIVATE: a project of the Chicago Loop Alliance Foundation.

properties.name: Faith In Humanity
properties.text: As human beings we are responsible for many of today’s problems. What we have done to the environment and Global Warming are addressed in this mural. Instead of focusing on the negative, the focus is going to be placed on a positive message. Even though we have been the cause of many of the problems, the most wonderful thing is we can also be the fix. Through the power of love, faith, hope and our intelligence we are capable of so many amazing things. Healing the earth and a better tomorrow can be two of those amazing things. It is my plan with this mural to remind the viewer of this and ask them to be part of the cure. With a lighthearted approach the animals of the earth are there to remind us that it is time to take action.

properties.name: Far Beyond
properties.text: Yollocalli Public Art Interns along with Teaching Artists Chema Skandal and Joseph J. Mora. The mural centers around a cougars head that is made up of many shapes giving it a very geometric look. The wall includes a wide array of colors and has a outterspace like background.

properties.name: Feed Your Child the Truth
properties.text: Completed 1994. Artist Bernard Williams. Feed Your Child the Truth is a celebration of African-American arts and culture. Mural images include African masks, Reverend Jessie 'Ma' Houston, and other community members. From 1994

The mural explores the theme of who is an other and who is considered a fellow. The mural deals with the issue of racism in the community. The end result is serious and meaningful but also fresh, colorful and energetic. From 1997

It features the status of Liberty on a red background with a First Responder spraying a hose. It is on the south facing wall of 4508 N Miwaukee and on the day of its dedication the roll call for the firehouse across the street was held on site.

properties.text: (Photo Credit: Sandra Steinbrecher) Collin van der Sluijs is a renowned painter and illustrator from The Netherlands, where he lives and works. Thanks to JK Equities and Vertical Gallery for partnering with the Wabash Arts Corridor and bringing Collin’s work to the district! “From Bloom to Doom” showcases two endangered birds from Illinois – the yellow-headed blackbird and the red-headed woodpecker – amongst native flowers.

properties.name: Fry

properties.text: (Photo Credit: Sandra Steinbrecher) Don’t Fret is a Chicago native and Columbia College alum and his practice includes drawing, painting, sculpture, performance and installation-based work both on the street and in the gallery space.

properties.name: Goralu, Czy Ci Nie Zal

properties.name: Indian Land Dancing
properties.word: Mural · 2009 · Cynthia Weiss, Tracy Van Duinen, and Todd Osborne
properties.text:
Created in 2009 on the north and south walls of the Foster Street underpass at Lake Shore Drive, Indian Land Dancing is an exceptional example of community-based artwork in Chicago. Initiated by Alderman Mary Ann Smith, the mural is meant to teach passersby about the past and present Native American Culture in the Great Lakes region. The three lead artists of the project—Cynthia Weiss, Tracy Van Duinen, and Todd Osborne—acted as facilitators for community discussions involving representatives from a cross-section of the Native American community as well as the Edgewater community, generally. Determined to create a mural that did not replicate generalizations about “Indian” culture, the design process took over two years of careful planning and community collaborations.

The result is a vibrant bricolage mosaic that utilizes ceramic tile, mirror, acrylic paint, and image transfer, among other media. The walls contain both large- and small-scale details so that both drivers and walkers can appreciate the mural. On the north wall one can see a mirrored DNA strand, a Native American iron worker, the mother embracing the next seven generations, a genealogy chart, and Tom Tom drums. On the south wall are phases of the moon, a thunderbird taking flight, a canoe rushing past a Native American lodge, sculpted corn, and sun imagery. These images balance themes commonly used to depict Native American culture with themes community members feel are seldom discussed but integral to contemporary discussions of Native American history. To represent family, modern pictures of children, families, poets, and activists became a centerpiece that grounds the bricolage. On the opposing wall, a collage of family photos collected by Native American participants offsets the grid-patterned centerpiece. Time and migration can be seen in the canoe, which is balanced by a skateboarder; the thunderbird, which is balanced by migrating geese; and the genealogy chart, which depicts the passing of generations.

properties.text: (Photo Credit: Dan Rest) "I created wispy butterfly wings that carry flowers adorned with motifs inspired by my roots and culture. The design inspiration comes from my family heirlooms-"carpetas tejidas" the delicate and intricate original crocheted designs of my grandmother and great grandmother. After watching some of Luzia, I reflected on the massive red papel picado that was used to incubate the twirling dancer ascending in one of the scenes as flower petals fell. Upon first sight it immediately made me think of the many designs links that make up my grandma’s doilies. I allowed the connection to guide the process of the mural's details. The dripping effect is a direct reflection of the water scenes and rather than make it a focal point, I wanted to create a subtle resemblance to the water while keeping it connected to my graffiti roots. Drips are common and often the most enjoyable parts of ink tags and natural spray paint abstracts when doing stylized letters. It is important for me to stay true to my Mexican & Graffiti culture for the two has been an integral part of my life and visual art form. I want to honor and elevate them in ways that don’t appropriate or erase the values or struggles that have endured through their evolution and survival.” The Magia de Luzia was curated and organized by Columbia College Chicago as part of the Wabash Arts Corridor Street Level Public Art Exhibition, and sponsored by Cirque du Soleil in honor of the production LUZIA in Chicago, Illinois.

properties.name: Life Cycle: Day + Night
properties.text: In 2022, Chicago-based interdisciplinary artist Gloria Talamantes (Talamantes) created the mural entitled, Life Cycle: Day + Night. The concept was based on Talamantes’ personal experiences of the nature path area in Lincoln Park during both daytime and nighttime. The mural is located at the Fullerton Pedestrian Underpass, across from the Peggy Notebaert Nature Museum. In 2012, the City of Chicago built a new bridge across the Lincoln Park Lagoon and created this pedestrian and cycling underpass. Both mural walls measure 110 feet long by 13 feet tall. Talamantes says of the new mural, “I believe the mural perfectly depicts the vibrancy of the many communities that exist in the space. From bug life, plant life and the frequency of bikers, skaters, trekkers, fisherman etc. who use the path, it embodies the diverse nature of the underpass path.” Talamantes finds that the mural is a great connector from one end of the park to another. It has received so many great responses from the local community, as well as Chicagoans and tourists alike. Talamantes reflects, “I painted this mural, while knowing that my Dad was terminally ill. He would ask me about the progress every day. I was able to find some comfort painting it during this difficult time.”

properties.name: Meander
properties.text:
Jim Bachor covers the contemporary urban fabric with the ancient technique of mosaic. Known for filling potholes with glass-and-mortar in Meander the artist elongated his scale to the width of a viaduct. He ordered over 1,000 pounds of ceramic tile from Italy to be set in a 90-foot mosaic.
 
Cut and laid out in the artist’s studio, the intricate but simple design shows three tulips—orange, yellow, and red—with their stems undulating along the mosaic’s expanse. From a distance, the flowers seem to be blowing in the breeze against an abstracted, rolling landscape. Up close, the incredible variety of tones and craftsmanship is apparent. Tiles that make up the orange tulip, for instance, include subtle differences of beige, yellow, and brown. Whether seen strolling by on foot or witnessed at the speed of a moving car, Bachor’s Meander enlivens the sterile space of a viaduct underpass.

properties.name: Patriotism in Everyday Life
properties.word: Mural · 2011 · Diana Berek, Chiara Padgett, Juan-Carlos Perez
properties.text: In 2011, the Chicago-based arts collective COMIGO was selected to paint the east Glenwood wall from Morse to Lunt, responding to a local call for artists on the theme of “Patriotism in Everyday Life”. COMIGO is Diana Berek, Chiara Padgett, and Juan-Carlos Perez, three Rogers Park artists who have had extensive experience in the visual arts as well as in mural and public arts. They first met when they worked on last year’s Mile of Murals project. About their response to the theme and their design for the wall, the collective says, “The core of our understanding of Patriotism in Everyday Life resides in this culturally negotiated understanding of “freedom”, i.e. in the perceptions, contradictions, questions, problems and issues that for more than 200 years continue to be challenged and re-defined. It is embedded in a persistent struggle to define and achieve freedom. It is distinctly opposed to casting American values in bellicose chauvinism, or a belief in national superiority. The American narrative is one of a deep striving toward personal success and individual freedom within a social, economic and political fabric of shared liberty and rights. The movement towards these ideals has been rocky, sometimes heroic and enlightened, sometimes ugly and violent, but the vision continues to inspire.”

properties.name: Prairie Fire
properties.text: Fire, both domestic and wild, is a recurring theme in my work. In this mural design, it functions as a metaphor of transformation and rebirth. Historically, prairie fires replenished nutrients to the soil encouraging new growth. This ecological fact echoes Chicago’s history which owes so much of its identity to the reconstruction that took place after the great fire and the innovation of the steel frame skyscraper. The mural is designed to be viewed in a linear, sequential manner as viewers walk along the alleyway and still work as a cohesive whole. The first glimpse of the mural from May Street would be of a drawn curtain revealing a copse of woods overlooking a prairie in the twilight of a dusk or dawn. Through the trees one can see a ribbon of bright yellow and orange fire which leads to dark billowing clouds of smoke in blues and purples over the open prairie. Beyond that the sky lightens and in the far distance, near the end of the mural, a city of skyscrapers rests on the horizon. The mural closes with another drawn curtain, thus framing the stage. The reference to a stage set and the use of dramatic lighting are also recurring motifs in my work. It functions as a nod to Chicago’s thriving and dynamic theater scene. It also helps place the wildfire in the context of a drama or metaphor, taking some of the edge off of what might otherwise be a foreboding subject matter to some. Nonetheless, I want the image to be somewhat ominous, but simultaneously beautiful, for it is that tension between fear and wonder, dark and light, that all of my work aims to wrestle with.

properties.name: Provocateurs Series
properties.text:

Four of the top names in subversive street art—Shepard Fairey, Cleon Peterson, POSE, and RETNA—have used the corridor as their “living urban canvas,” injecting provocative, large-scale artworks into one of Chicago’s major emerging art scenes. The outdoor art, as part of the Wabash Arts Corridor, will remain indefinitely.
“Street art and graffiti are no longer strictly defined as vandalism and deserves to be recognized as a valid and important art genre,” said Shepard Fairey, artist and curator of The Provocateurs. “It challenges the notion that public space should be dominated by advertising and government signage. Columbia College and the City of Chicago have enthusiastically supported our outdoor mural project.”

properties.name: Rush More
properties.text:
This large-scale mural on the Chicago Cultural Center building is the culmination the city’s Year of Public Art. Made by internationally renowned Artist Kerry James Marshall, the 132 x 100-foot mural—the largest artwork he has ever designed or created—honors 20 women who have shaped the city’s vibrant arts and cultural landscape. In explaining his choice of women, Kerry James Marshall said, “In the history of monuments you have very few that represent women, but in the history of Chicago you have very many women that played key roles in establishing culture here. . . . My idea was to make a Forest Rushmore acknowledging the contribution of 20 women who’ve worked to shape the cultural landscape of the city, past and present.” The mural, executed by Artist Jeff Zimmerman, consists of trees as totems decorated by the women’s faces on the bottom. Up above are the park-like treetops, birds, a yellow-and-blue sun, and a ribbon that floats throughout the mural. 

The cross-cultural, multi-generational list of women include (left to right) actress and cofounder of Dearborn Homes Youth Drama Workshop Cheryl Lynn Bruce; founder of Chicago Children’s Theatre Jacqueline Russell; former Chicago First lady and founder of After School Matters Maggie Daley; founder of the DuSable Museum of African American History Margaret Burroughs; founder of Little Black Pearl Monica Haslip; television host and producer Oprah Winfrey; poet Gwendolyn Brooks; former Chicago cultural affairs commissioner Lois Weisberg; actress/writer, and cofounder of Collaboraction theater, Sandra Delgado; journalist and writer Achy Obejas; founder of eta Creative Arts Foundation Abena Joan Brown; Poetry magazine founder Harriet Monroe; founder of Black Ensemble Theater Jackie Taylor; founder and Artistic director of Chicago Shakespeare Theater Barbara Gaines; former director of the Renaissance Society Suzanne Ghez; dancer and president of Muntu Dance Theatre of Chicago Joan Gray; dancer, choreographer, and founder of Ruth Page Center for the Arts Ruth Page; writer Sandra Ciseneros; Artist and cofounder of the AfricCobra collective Barbara Jones-Hogu; Janes Saks, founder of Project & and the Ellen stone Belic Institute for the study of Women and Gender in the Arts and Media.

The mural is funded by Murals of Acceptance, whose goal is to bring art to all people in a free public setting.

properties.name: Spread Your Wings and Fly
properties.text: Abre Tus Alas y Vuela will be an immersive, interactive, and engaging mural that ignites the imagination and sparks creativity and curiosity with every encounter. It will inspire us to dream, to explore, to experience the childlike wonder and awe that connects us all at our core. It will serve as a reminder of the innate love and wisdom that is felt when we interact with nature, and the profound way we are moved by the beauty and diversity of the natural world. With endless opportunities for photos and â€œInstagrammableâ€� moments with children and adults alike, the artwork will become a backdrop for treasured family moments, memories, and milestones. A place of discovery, learning, connection and teaching moments for parents, children, friends, and families. It will become an opportunity to connect with others, to laugh, have fun, and make lasting memories. Inspired from one of my fondest childhood memories, I will create and paint on each wall a numbered correlation key of animals, plants, and identifiable objects that kids can search for and identify as a fun, engaging, and educational activity to explore and learn. It will be an invitation for everyone to explore, discover, and experience a magical wonderland of forests, nature, wildlife, flora, and fauna. Vibrating with a rich diversity of life, and bursting with new surprises and details to discover at every turn, it will be an exciting place for children to visit and spend time traveling through. With a warm and welcoming gold glow, visitors will feel safe, secure, and comforted by the beauty and inclusivity of Mother Natureâ€™s unconditional embrace. The metallic gold paint will sparkle and shine adding a deeper level of magic and majesty, evoking a quiet sense of serenity and connection to the Divine. Whether passing by on foot, two wheels, or four, it will be a uniquely personal and beautiful journey of remembering. Remembering the source of who we are, individually, and as one. Remembering to dream, to soar, and to be the best that we can be.

properties.name: Take My Hand, Precious Lord
properties.text: The mural *"Take My Hand, Precious Lord"* beautifully honors Thomas Dorsey, the father of gospel music, with a poignant and reverent depiction of his legacy. Radiant light surrounds him, symbolizing the divine connection he forged through his music. Elements of the song "Take My Hand, Precious Lord" swirl around the mural in ethereal patterns, connecting Dorsey to both his church roots and his lasting influence on gospel music worldwide. The piece radiates warmth and reverence, capturing Dorsey's profound contribution to both faith and music.

properties.name: The Artist
properties.text: Visible from the Green Line, the (The Artist) mural, commissioned by Jake Troyli, an artist known for exploring the construction of otherness and the commodification of Black and Brown bodies, stands as a beacon of empowerment. After experiencing SkyARTâ€™s transformative youth programs, Troyli connected deeply with young artists aged 7 to 13, recognizing the profound impact of SkyARTâ€™s mission to provide free art programming and art therapy. In collaboration with SkyWAY artists, Troyli crafted a powerful message for Chicago's youth: to forge their own paths and create their own possibilities. What began as simple doodles evolved into a breathtaking masterpiece, portraying a young man of color, donning in Troyliâ€™s iconic afro and Chicago Jordans, climbing a ladder while painting vast clouds into a bright blue sky. This towering figure, a symbol of self-determination and the creation of one's own reality, proudly overlooks the city from the Green Line. Doze uses simple graphic imagery combined with complex layering and color movement to show the constant flux of realities, addressing the present moment and connecting it with the past and future. Light beams emanating from individual faces map the manifestation of ideas and the future, and arms are raised for the revolutions and uprisings. Yet despite this variance, or perhaps in spite of it, there exudes a uniform strength of pattern, repetition and interconnectedness of and between individuals, each individual being part and parcel of a larger community, albeit humanity. Everyone exists as an equal agent of change unto themselves. Everyone bears witness to humankind's grander narrative of a shared spiritual past, present and future, a genetic chain spanning throughout time immemorial, dividing and duplicating into a spectrum of multitudinous colors and relations, of multitudinous humanities and gods."

properties.name: Urbs in Horto
properties.text:
"URBS IN HORTO, Latin for 'City in a Garden,' is the official city motto of Chicago. In order to capture the essence of this phrase, I portrayed a lush bouquet of Chrysanthemums, Roses, Echinacea, and prairie grasses. Each of these blooms can be found in the city and serves a purpose in the bouquet apart from making a beautiful arrangement. Chrysanthemums are Chicago's official flower, so they are featured most prominently in the mural. Roses are universally recognizable and loved, but they were also Anne Hewlett Fuller's favorite, and the bloom that the famous Chicagoan architect and designer Buckminster Fuller gave her in courtship. Echinacea and prairie grasses are both found growing wild in Chicago, a nod to the abundance of beautiful wild foliage in Illinois. The symbolic blooms coupled with the title of the piece honor the city's close and nuanced relationship with nature."

URBS IN HORTO is part of the Lakeview Public Art Program, an initiative
of Special Service Area 27 and its 501(c)(3) non-profit partner organization, Friends of Lakeview which showcases original works of art by innovative artists throughout the West Lakeview neighborhood.

The mosaic also seeks to showcase the diversity in the area, make the viaduct more pedestrian friendly, and highlight that many ward residents are civil servants, including police and fire fighters.

properties.name: Woodlawn Gateway at 65th
properties.text: Green Star Movement, with the help of approximately 500 volunteers, created this mosaic to celebrate the Woodlawn neighborhood and its culture. Elaborate portraits of notable figures, including Barack Obama, Michelle Obama, and singer Minnie Riperton are shaped out of tile. Photographs embedded in the material memorialize other former residents—including Emmett Till and Muhammad Ali. Further highlighting Woodlawn’s rich history, imagery from the front page of the Chicago Crusader, a newspaper headquartered in the neighborhood, is prominently displayed within the mosaic.

properties.name: Year Round 2020
properties.text: “Year Round 2019” is an artwork by Mauricio Ramirez that that tells a story of how Chicago embraces all four seasons. “One of the most unique things about Chicago is how the seasons highly influence the activity throughout the city. I have chosen to depict this narrative by abstractly using geometrical shapes that hold color that corresponds to their season. All through the mural, you can see how the seasons of color playfully interact with each other.” The artwork will be painted on brick, with some basic site preparation needed including power washing the entirety of the wall.

properties.name: Yes, And
properties.text: The Revival is an improv theater located at the site where the artform was invented in 1955 (see The Compass Players). The core philosophy of improv is known as "Yes And." This mural is an homage to the artform and features local community practitioners of improv.

properties.name: Your Place or Mime?
properties.text: This mural is dedicated to "2019 Year of Chicago Theatre" depicting two mimes that each represent happy and sad emotions through theatre. The skull is a representation of spiritual connectivity, a signature mark by Chicago artist, Afrokilla. This mural was created for ACTIVATE: a project of the Chicago Loop Alliance Foundation.
